::: {.hero}
```{=html}

<p class="lede">A free, hands-on course in modern natural language processing —
written for engineers and statisticians who don't have a computer-science
background, and taken from a live course at METU (ODTÜ), Ankara.</p>
<p class="meta">Interactive · Open source · Updated as the field moves

  <a class="btn btn-anlp-primary" href="chapters/01-why-nlp-now.html">Start reading →</a>
```

:::

The title above is not decoration — it is the book's first lesson. That is
roughly how a language model actually reads: text is [split into subword
tokens]{.hl}, and everything else — embeddings, attention, generation — is
built on top of that stream. By the end of this book you will know exactly
what happens to those chips, and you will have built working systems on top
of models that process them.

All thirty-nine chapters and six appendices are drafted, in both editions.
Chapters marked ⚡ ship with working in-browser widgets, and the
[changelog](#updates) records what changed and when.

## How this book works

**It assumes statistics, not CS.** If you can read a regression table, you
have every prerequisite. New machinery is introduced by analogy to things you
already know — attention is a [learned weighted average]{.hl}, embeddings are
coordinates, fine-tuning is re-estimation.

**It is interactive.** Key ideas come with widgets that run entirely in your
browser — drag a temperature slider, watch a probability distribution reshape
itself. No installation, no GPU. Start with the
[attention head explorer](chapters/07-transformers.qmd), then the
[sampling policy explorer](chapters/18-decoding-structured-output.qmd).

**It is executable.** Code chapters ship as real, runnable Python. Colab
notebooks are not published yet; until they are, copy the code blocks into
your own environment and break things there (see
[the setup appendix](appendices/a-setup.qmd#sec-setup-colab)).

**It is alive.** The field moves; the book moves with it. Watch the
repository or subscribe to the changelog to see what changed between visits.
Found an error? Every page has an *Edit* link — fixes arrive as pull requests.

## For instructors

The book is deliberately larger than one semester. The fourteen-week plan in
@sec-syllabus assigns twenty-four of the thirty-nine chapters — all of Part I,
most of Parts II and IV, half of Parts III and V, the security and guardrails
chapters of Part VI, and the capstone case study — and lists the fifteen it
cuts, with reasons. Parts V–VII are built so an agents-focused or
production-focused second course can be cut from the same material. Slides,
homework notebooks, and a suggested grading scheme are being added chapter by
chapter. The text is CC BY 4.0 and the code MIT: reuse it, translate it, remix
it — just keep the attribution.

| 2026-09 | Chapter 39 *Case Study: Building an Enterprise Agent Platform* drafted — deliberately with **no measurement of its own**. It assembles a support platform for a Turkish e-commerce company out of numbers made elsewhere in the book, which is the exercise the capstone asks for: latency from the prefill/decode split, token volume from **890 prompt tokens against 53 generated**, telemetry from **4.8 spans and 3,167 bytes per run**, eval sizing from **13.4 points at 100 items**, guardrail precision from **40% pattern-only**, and risk from a **92–100%** attack success rate. Six architecture decisions are recorded with the alternative that was rejected and why, and the platform failures are dated rather than listed — a shared tool breaks someone at the second team, nobody knows what exists at the fifth agent, the platform team is the bottleneck at the tenth. |
| 2026-09 | Chapter 38 *Governance, Compliance and FinOps* drafted — with the legal dates read off the current instruments rather than recalled, because two of them had moved eight weeks earlier. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 deferred Annex III high-risk obligations to **2 December 2027** and Annex I to **2 August 2028** while prohibitions, GPAI duties and Article 50 transparency kept their original dates, so "the AI Act was delayed" is wrong for most teams' actual obligations; KVKK Article 9, as rewritten by Law 7499, requires a standard contract to be **notified to the Authority within five business days of signature**. The measurement is the cost lever everyone recommends and nobody sizes: escalating **20%** of a 100-item extraction suite from a 3B model to a 27B one took field accuracy from **92.40% to 97.00%** against 100.00% for the large model alone, costing $(1+0.2K)/K$ of the large-model bill. The row that teaches most is the last one — a 9B model passed the format validator on **100 of 100** items while being correct on **97.80%** of fields, so its cascade escalated **0%** and saved nothing. Well-formedness stops correlating with correctness as soon as the model is reliably well-formed. |
| 2026-09 | Chapter 37 *Guardrails and Human Oversight* drafted — one measurement with no model in it at all, and it is about what a filter deletes rather than what it catches. Four Turkish PII detectors over 480 messages with **360 planted national IDs and 540 eleven-digit decoys**: an eleven-digit pattern is **40.0% precise at 100% recall**, because a Turkish mobile written without spaces is also eleven digits. Adding the published checksum takes precision to **99.0%** and costs **15.3 points of recall** — and that loss is *mechanically equal* to the corpus's typo rate, so what the validator removes is exactly the mistyped identifiers, which are still personal data sitting in your logs. A context check fails on different items, so their union reaches **99.1% precision at 93.6% recall**. IBAN is the counterexample that makes the rule: the pattern is already 100% precise, so its checksum buys **zero** and discards **12.5%** of real ones. Validate where the pattern is ambiguous; use a checksum to rank confidence, not to filter. |
| 2026-09 | Chapter 36 *Security for Tool-Using Agents* drafted — and the first attempt at the detection measurement returned zero on every category, which looked like a finding and was not one yet. Varying the question instead of trusting one phrasing produced the real result. The attack is not exotic: plain Turkish instructions planted in a support ticket made an agent email an attacker-chosen address on **25 of 25 runs**, with a system-notice framing and an invisible HTML comment each working **23 of 25** and a clean control at zero. Asking the same model to spot the payload, across four phrasings and seven documents: two phrasings never fired on any of **175** documents, one fired on **everything including clean tickets**, and the only one with a usable false-positive rate caught **11 of 75** real payloads — **14.7%**, and **0%** of the hidden variant. One result runs against intuition and is kept: the crudest obfuscation was detected **20/25**, more often than the plain payload at 8/25. |
| 2026-09 | Chapter 35 *Evaluation in Production* drafted — measuring a question the book had not yet asked: how far does an eval score move when *nothing* changed? Five identical runs of a 100-item Turkish extraction suite spanned **0.60 points** of field accuracy, which is small enough to gate on and contradicts the folklore. The central result is the edit nobody would question: reordering six prompt rules with none added, removed or reworded cost **3.40 points of field accuracy and 9.20 of exact match**, about six times the noise floor, with the entire regression inside one field — and the per-field breakdown gave it a mechanism, since **every wrong `day` under both prompts was the leading digits of the amount**. The gate design follows: blocking whenever the new score is lower falsely blocks **42.5%** of no-op changes at 100 items and *gets worse as the suite grows*, while a 1-point threshold gives **4.3%** false blocks and still catches the reordering **99.4%** of the time. |
| 2026-09 | Chapter 34 *Observability for Agents* drafted — with the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions read off the specification, which is itself the finding: they moved into their own repository in 2026, and of the marked items in the current span document **286 are `Development` against 22 `Stable`**, with no tagged release at all. Use them, pin the version, record the pin. The measurement is what a trace costs before you turn content logging on: **4.8 spans and 3,167 bytes per run**, of which **48.3% was prompt and completion text** — and that was on 301-token prompts. Holding the structure fixed and scaling the text to a realistic 890 tokens gives **73.4% content**, and at 4,258-token contexts **93.0%**. Whether you log prompts is a four- to fourteen-fold decision about your monitoring bill, and it is a privacy decision at the same time. |
| 2026-09 | Chapter 33 *Deployment Topologies and Reliability* drafted — 48 calls settling a design question people assume rather than measure: when you retry an agent step, do you get the same tool call? Asked to *notify whoever needs to know* about a failed pump, a model produced **five different recipient addresses across eight retries** at temperature 0.7, every one of them invented. So a retry did not repeat the action, it performed a different one — which is why an idempotency key cannot be a hash of the tool arguments, the design usually chosen by default. Temperature 0 made all eight retries byte-identical, including the run that deterministically invented an address: reproducible and still wrong, and not a guarantee on a hosted API anyway. The chapter also names the tools that have no compensating action, which is the row that decides where an approval gate goes. |
| 2026-09 | Chapter 32 *The Gateway Layer* drafted — and the semantic-cache measurement exposed a defect in the instrument, which is the more useful half. Fifteen labelled support-query pairs embedded with `nomic-embed-text`: the most similar pair in the whole set is **a sentence and its negation at 0.982**, while a genuinely identical question sits at **0.609**, so the two classes overlap completely and no single threshold separates them. The table is lowercased, and it did not start that way — written naturally, *business hours on Monday* and *on Sunday* came back at cosine **1.000**, byte-identical vectors. Following that produced a reproducible finding about the tool: under `ollama` 0.24.0 that embedder maps **every capitalised word to one constant token**, so *Monday*, *Cat*, *Ankara* and *XYZZY* are the same vector and *Cat sat on the mat* equals *Dog sat on the mat*. A cache built on it would have answered Sunday's question with Monday's answer, forever, logging nothing. It surfaced only because a pair that had to score low scored highest. |
| 2026-09 | Chapter 31 *Serving and Inference Infrastructure* drafted, opening Part VI — about forty short requests on a laptop, because the quantities that matter are ratios. Prefill runs at roughly **2,000 tokens per second** against decode at **185**, so reading a token is about eleven times cheaper than writing one, and at 7,455 tokens of context **90.7% of the wall clock was over before the first character appeared** — a number streaming cannot touch. Long context is charged twice: decode also fell from **185 to 139 tokens per second** as the window filled. The KV cache arithmetic makes "will it fit?" a question about context length rather than model size — **112 KiB per token** means a 131k window on a 2.0 GB model is **14 GiB of cache, seven times the weights**. And prompt caching is the first lever and not a subtle one: warm prefill was **flat at 13–18 ms regardless of prompt length**, 126× on prefill and 8.2× on the whole request at 4,258 tokens. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 30 *Evaluating Agents* drafted — Part V closes by scoring the same thirty runs two ways, and the result corrected the claim the chapter started from. Trajectory evaluation caught runs outcome evaluation passed on **one run in thirty**, not many: when a system takes a bad path it usually gets the wrong answer too, so the two metrics mostly agree on *which* runs fail. It earns its place through what outcome hides instead — a system at **36.7% accuracy** was making **7.10 tool calls for a task needing 2**, with **70% of them repeats**, and hitting its step cap on **63.3%** of runs, which means those were unfinished runs rather than wrong answers, a different repair entirely. And the cost correction: on raw tokens that system looked 1.9× more expensive than the structured loop; per *correct* answer it was **5.1×**, so the outcome-blind figure most comparisons quote understated the gap by nearly three-fold. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 29 *Agentic RAG* drafted — with a single-hop control, so the chapter is not measuring only the case its subject wins. Classic RAG scored **0.0% on thirty two-hop questions** whose answer key exists only inside another document, while scoring **100%** on single-hop versions of the same facts: most likely a structural ceiling rather than a ranking problem (the second document's rank was not recorded), so a reranker over the same candidates does not reach it. Agentic retrieval **removed the ceiling without clearing it** — 0% to **30%**, at **6.6× the tokens** and 3.43 rounds of a three-round budget, about 3,475 tokens per correct answer. And on single-hop questions the loop bought nothing and cost **1.15×**, which is the case that dominates real traffic. The conclusion is therefore a router rather than an architecture: default to the pipeline, detect the questions whose answer depends on a key the question cannot contain, and send only those into the loop. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 28 *Multi-Agent Patterns* drafted — the cost question answered with arithmetic rather than a diagram, using constants measured earlier in the book. Splitting work across a coordinator and three specialists **costs 1.20× on six steps with 200-token results** — more expensive, because the per-agent fixed cost is paid three extra times — and **saves two thirds on twenty-four steps with 3,000-token results** (862,800 tokens as one agent against 291,510 as three), because a single agent carries every observation through every later call. So the dial is how much material the work produces, not how hard it is. The chapter then says what the saving costs: the coordinator sees summaries *because that is the mechanism*, so it reasons about a lossy compression, and three specialists at 90% give somewhere between 70% and 90% — about 73% only if their errors are independent — before the coordinator's own synthesis — the step chapter 23 measured as the first to break. Read-heavy work parallelises; write-heavy work becomes a distributed system with lost updates that raise no error. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 27 *MCP and Agent Interoperability* drafted — and written from the specification rather than from memory, which changed the chapter. As of revision **2026-07-28** the base protocol is **stateless, self-contained requests** with per-request negotiation, not the stateful `initialize` handshake a 2025 account describes, and that is what lets a remote server scale horizontally. **Sampling, Roots, Logging and Dynamic Client Registration are all deprecated** with published migration paths — a narrowing worth reading as design commentary, since Sampling and Roots were both ways for a server to reach back into the host. Servers now offer three features and clients offer one. The cost section is arithmetic on the official filesystem server's 14 published tools: **89 tokens per definition**, paid on every call, so three installed servers spend about **75,000 tokens across a twenty-step session** before anyone says anything — softened by prompt caching, but invisible and multiplicative. And the security framing follows from chapter 24: a tool description is prompt text shipped by a third party, which the spec itself says to treat as untrusted, giving tool poisoning, rug-pulls and cross-server shadowing. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 26 *Memory Architectures* drafted — one small probe, and it settles a design question cheaply. Thirty invented contradictions (the user preferred email in March and phone in July): with both facts present and **no timestamps the model chose the newer one 0% of the time**, hedging on 83.3%; adding timestamps got it to 33.3%; adding an explicit "prefer the most recent" rule got it to **83.3%**, with the remaining one answer in six hedging rather than choosing — none picked the older fact. So contradiction resolution belongs in the retrieval layer, not the prompt — resolve first, inject one fact. The chapter also separates three memories by *how they fail*: working memory loudly when the window fills, episodic slowly as volume degrades retrieval, and **semantic silently**, returning a March fact confidently in July. Facts belong in rows keyed by user and attribute; episodes belong in an index — putting facts in a vector store is the common production mistake, because it makes update and delete impossible by name, and the bill arrives at the first erasure request. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 25 *Context Engineering* drafted — and the degradation claim needed the literature rather than a laptop. A local probe on an aggregation task was **flat** (100% → 93.3% → 88.3% → 88.3% → 96.7% as distractors grew to 11k tokens, intervals overlapping), matching chapter 20's needle result. Both of my tests allowed the model to *literal-match* the answer, which is exactly the crutch @modarressi2025nolima removed: on needles with minimal lexical overlap, **11 of 13 models claiming 128K contexts fall below half their short-context baseline at 32K**, GPT-4o from **99.3% to 69.7%**. @hsieh2024ruler reaches the same place — near-perfect on vanilla needle-in-a-haystack, large drops as soon as the task needs multi-hop tracing or aggregation, with only half of 17 models holding up at 32K. The operational rule: a model's advertised context length is a capacity, not a competence, and the reassuring test is the one designed-in lexical overlap makes easy. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 25 *Context Engineering* drafted — and it is the first chapter where the decisive evidence is published rather than mine, deliberately. Two local attempts to measure context degradation both returned **flat curves**: chapter 20's needle test scored 100% across 640 queries to 16,775 tokens, and a harder version here — find two invented figures and add them — stayed within noise from 0 to 60 distractor documents (100% → 88.3% → 96.7%, intervals overlapping). Both missed the effect for the same reason, and it is the reason most in-house evaluations miss it: **the question contained the same rare string as the answer**, so the model could match instead of infer. @modarressi2025nolima removes exactly that crutch and finds **11 of 13 models below half their short-context baseline at 32K**, GPT-4o from 99.3% to 69.7%; @hsieh2024ruler finds only half of 17 models holding up at the 32K they advertise, with near-perfect vanilla needle scores throughout. So an advertised context length is a capacity, not a competence — and the test that would reassure you is the one designed-in lexical overlap makes easy. The rest of the chapter is the budget framing (every token is re-sent on every model call, so fixed costs are multiplied by step count), compaction with a facts list exempt by rule, sub-agent isolation as the largest single lever, just-in-time retrieval by hit rate, the filesystem as external memory, and where chunk-and-embed fails outright. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 24 *Tool Design as API Design* drafted — two experiments, and both landed away from where the effort usually goes. Four versions of one tool, differing only in how they are described: moving a parameter from a free string to an **enum took correct calls from 25% to 100%**, and adding careful prose descriptions on top added **nothing measurable**. The opaque variant failed in the way worth fearing — it did not make wrong calls, it made **no call 41.7% of the time** and answered from parametric memory instead, in confident invented prose. Without an enum the model echoes the user's vocabulary straight into the API (*mali buyukluk*, *ekip mevcudu*, *takvim*) including **`bütçe` where the API wants `butce`**, which is chapter 16's problem arriving inside a function signature. The second experiment holds everything fixed and changes only what a failing tool returns: an actionable message that names the invalid value and lists the valid ones took recovery from **1.7% to 100%**, while a **stack trace was the worst of the four** at 81.7% abandonment — worse than a bare "Error" — because it looks authoritative and offers no path forward. The dominant failure after an error is giving up, not looping. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 23 *Agent Anatomy* drafted — Part V opens by writing the whole agent out in fourteen lines and then measuring where it fails. On a task with unguessable answers reachable only through a tool, accuracy fell **100% → 96% → 80% → 68% → 40%** as the task went from one lookup to five — while **tool use stayed perfect** at every step count: exactly the right number of calls, none malformed, none hitting the step cap. The loop is not what breaks; aggregation over what the loop collected is, which redirects where you debug. The cost story is separate and surprising: the native loop used **2.0 model calls at every step count** because the model batches its tool calls, so five times the work cost 1.52× the tokens, while a hand-rolled text protocol paid 3.5× the model calls for the same work. That protocol also lost at every step count, by up to **60 accuracy points**, and failed to terminate on **60% of one-lookup tasks** — retrieving the answer at step 0 and then repeating the call until the budget ran out, because in a text protocol the answer command competes with the tool command while a structured API makes stopping a different kind of action. Two of my own errors are documented in place: a prompt whose placeholder syntax the model read literally, and a quadratic-cost claim the measurement refuted. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 22 *Evaluating LLM Systems* drafted — the chapter for the statistics audience, and it opens by pricing the thing everyone skips. Against a system that is right 80% of the time, a **30-item eval set can detect no difference at all** at 80% power: even a replacement that is right *every* time reaches only 75%. A hundred items detects 13.4 points, a thousand detects 4.8, and most real improvements are 2–5 — so small eval sets are for finding failure modes and large ones for deciding what ships. Pairing helps in proportion to agreement: at 10% disagreement McNemar more than doubles power at n = 200, at 30% it is a wash, and at **40% it is worse** than the unpaired test, because it discards every agreement. Then the judge audit, and the result that matters: both `qwen3.5:9b` and `gemma3:27b` scored **100%** on the identical-text control everyone runs — and then the small judge **flipped its verdict on 38% of items** when the order was swapped and sat at chance (51.7%) on the real comparison, while the large one flipped on 15% and reached 74.2%; all three probe differences significant at n = 60. Verbosity bias did not reproduce in either. Writing this chapter also caught two errors in my own analysis — a framing that made pairing look harmful, and a binary search that reported its own ceiling as a result — both documented in place. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 21 *Multimodal Models* drafted — chapter 16's control moved into pixels, and it finds the same pattern with no text pipeline involved. On professionally translated sentence pairs rendered as page images in one font at four sizes, **Turkish costs about 5× the character error rate of English at every resolution** — 0.26% against 0.04% at 34 px, **6.67% against 1.33%** at 11 px — on identical content, with no tokenizer, stemmer or `lower()` anywhere near it. The same content needs **1.29× as many word tokens in English but only 1.02× as many characters**, so a word n-gram metric has 29% fewer slots in Turkish and every error costs more: the identical semantic error charges **14.90 BLEU in Turkish against 12.65 in English**, while chrF charges 3.05 against 5.34 — the two metrics disagree 4.89× in Turkish and 2.37× in English. Decoding turned out to be a task setting rather than a model setting: beam-4 scores 30.17 and a chat-default temperature of 1.0 scores **14.34** on the same model. The most surprising result is not about a model: the **human reference summaries assert unsupported content in 33–57% of cases against 2–7% for a prompted LLM**, so ROUGE on this corpus rewards hallucination and fine-tuning on it would teach a model to invent.
